I would keep things simple and stay with the main local pattern: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same land. In Quzhou County, that rotation is what I trust most because I know the work rhythm, the market is familiar, and the land and water conditions fit it better than trying something risky. With my education level and the need to control labor and cash, I would rather run a steady grain system than chase a complicated cash crop. I would use improved wheat seed and hybrid maize seed, put most of my fertilizer into the base application plus one key topdressing period, irrigate only at the most important growth stages, and keep pesticide spraying limited to the main disease and insect windows. For wheat, I would focus on strong seedlings, one spring nitrogen topdressing, and irrigation around jointing and grain filling if moisture is short. After wheat harvest, I would move quickly into summer maize, using no-tillage direct seeding to save time and hold soil moisture, then manage weeds early, topdress nitrogen around the big flare stage, and protect the crop during peak pest pressure. I would do this because it is the most dependable way for me to protect yield, control cost, and reduce management mistakes over the full year.
